generic: Eptacog Alfa (activated) - recombinant coagulation factor VIIa
cls: Recombinant activated coagulation factor VIIa (bypassing agent)
quick: Hemophilia A/B with inhibitors: 90 mcg/kg IV bolus every 2 hours until hemostasis (regimen varies by indication)
Limited data; use only if clearly needed
Unknown if excreted in milk; use with caution
Use with caution in hepatic impairment / liver disease
Clinical hemostasis (not routine coagulation assays); signs of thrombosis
summary: Eptacog alfa (activated) is recombinant human coagulation factor VIIa (rFVIIa) used as a bypassing agent to treat and prevent bleeding. It is indicated for bleeding episodes and surgery in hemophilia A or B patients with inhibitors, acquired hemophilia, congenital factor VII deficiency, and Glanzmann thrombasthenia refractory to platelets. It promotes hemostasis by activating the coagulation cascade at the site of tissue injury, largely independent of factors VIII and IX. The principal serious risk is thrombosis (arterial and venous thromboembolic events), so it must be used cautiously in patients with thrombotic risk.
indications: Treatment of bleeding episodes and perioperative management in adults and children with hemophilia A or B with inhibitors to factor VIII or IX
Treatment of bleeding episodes and perioperative management in patients with acquired hemophilia
Treatment of bleeding episodes and perioperative management in patients with congenital factor VII deficiency
Treatment of bleeding and perioperative management in Glanzmann thrombasthenia refractory to platelet transfusions (with or without antibodies to platelets)

dosage.t: Every 2 hours until hemostasis achieved, then interval may be extended (3-6 hourly)
dosage.n: Alternative single dose of 270 mcg/kg has been used; individualize

dosage.t: Repeat every 2 hours during surgery, then every 2-6 hours postoperatively per procedure severity
dosage.n: Continue based on bleeding and procedure type
Lower doses than hemophilia inhibitor indication

dosage.t: Every 2 hours (at least 3 doses) to maintain hemostasis

admin: Reconstitute the powder with the supplied diluent following the package instructions; do not shake violently
Administer by slow intravenous bolus injection over 2 to 5 minutes
Do not mix with infusion solutions or give as a continuous infusion unless specified
Use reconstituted solution promptly; discard per labeling
Dose and frequency are individualized to the type of bleed, indication, and clinical response
moa: Eptacog alfa is recombinant activated factor VII (FVIIa). At pharmacologic doses it binds to exposed tissue factor at the site of vascular injury and directly activates factor X to Xa on the surface of activated platelets, generating a thrombin burst that converts fibrinogen to fibrin and produces a stable hemostatic plug. This action largely bypasses the need for factors VIII and IX, allowing hemostasis in patients with inhibitors against those factors.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to eptacog alfa, mouse, hamster, or bovine proteins (depending on product)
relative: Conditions predisposing to thromboembolism (atherosclerotic disease, crush injury, septicemia, DIC, advanced age)
Concomitant use of activated/non-activated prothrombin complex concentrates (increased thrombotic risk)
monitor: Clinical signs and symptoms of thrombosis (arterial and venous)
Disseminated intravascular coagulation in at-risk patients

preg: There are limited data on use in pregnant women. Eptacog alfa should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed and the benefit justifies any potential risk.
lact: It is not known whether eptacog alfa is excreted in human milk. Because many proteins are excreted in milk, caution should be exercised when administering to a nursing woman.
renal: No specific dosage adjustment for renal impairment has been established; pharmacokinetics are not substantially dependent on renal clearance. Individualize therapy.
hepatic: Use with caution in patients with liver disease, who may have a higher risk of coagulation disturbances; clinical monitoring of hemostasis is advised.

major: Activated prothrombin complex concentrates (aPCC) or prothrombin complex concentrates - avoid concomitant use; increased risk of thrombotic complications
Recombinant factor XIII (potential interaction; avoid concomitant administration unless specified)
moderate: Antifibrinolytics and other procoagulants (additive thrombotic risk)
interactions.diagnostics: Affects coagulation assays (e.g., shortens prothrombin time); routine coagulation parameters do not reliably correlate with clinical hemostasis

common: Decreased plasma fibrinogen / changes in coagulation tests
serious: Arterial thrombotic events (myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction/stroke)
rare: Development of inhibitory antibodies to factor VII (especially in factor VII deficiency)
Acute myocardial infarction in patients without prior coronary disease
emergency: Signs of stroke or myocardial infarction
Signs of pulmonary embolism (sudden dyspnea, chest pain)

monitoring: Clinical assessment of hemostatic response (laboratory coagulation tests do not reliably predict efficacy)
Signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation in patients with predisposing conditions
Hypersensitivity reactions during and after administration
Factor VII inhibitor antibodies in factor VII deficiency
counsel: This medicine is given by injection into a vein to control or prevent bleeding
Seek emergency care for chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, weakness on one side, slurred speech, or leg pain/swelling - these can signal a clot
Tell your team about any allergy to mouse, hamster, or cow proteins
Report rash, itching, wheeze, or swelling during or after the injection
Keep follow-up appointments to assess bleeding control
pk: Hemostatic effect begins rapidly after intravenous bolus
Peak FVIIa activity immediately after the bolus injection
Approximately 2-3 hours (shorter, around 1.3 hours, in children)
Short - repeat dosing every 2-6 hours is usually required
Store refrigerated (2-8 C) or per label; protect from light; use reconstituted solution promptly
pearls: A bypassing agent - it works largely independent of factors VIII and IX, making it useful in hemophilia patients with inhibitors
Thrombosis (arterial and venous) is the principal serious risk; weigh carefully in patients with cardiovascular disease, DIC, or other prothrombotic states
Avoid concomitant prothrombin complex concentrates (activated or not) because of additive thrombotic risk
Routine coagulation tests do not reliably predict efficacy - dose to clinical hemostasis
Short half-life mandates frequent (every 2 hours) dosing during active bleeding until control is achieved
missed: Eptacog alfa is given as needed to treat or prevent bleeding under medical supervision, not on a fixed self-administered schedule. If a planned dose during ongoing bleeding management is delayed, give it as soon as possible and continue the prescribed interval; contact the treatment center for guidance if bleeding recurs.
overdose: Dose-limiting toxicity has not been clearly defined, but overdose increases the risk of thromboembolic complications. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive: discontinue, monitor closely for arterial and venous thrombosis, and treat thrombotic or coagulopathic complications (including disseminated intravascular coagulation) as they arise.
